brief.head: The moving bottleneck
brief.text: On a long climb, Ajay Shah said, the body complains about whatever is scarcest: plenty of oxygen and the thighs whine; strong legs and the lungs do. {035-C03}

brief.head: Teammates, not staff
brief.text: Treat the mountain crew as teammates, not hotel staff, Shah said. If they run out of creamer, take the black coffee, and do it with a smile. {035-C10}

brief.head: Mind the dinner
brief.text: Hiking with a CGM, Shah found that Maggi, white rice and maida still spike blood sugar. Dinner matters most, he said, because afterwards you’re not burning. {035-C13}

brief.head: Physicists on foot
brief.text: Lots of physics people go hiking, Shah noted, a “funny correlation”: you experience gravity, light and air at a different level altogether. {#physics}

brief.head: Every fall a story
brief.text: Setbacks on the trail become good stories later, Shah said. Amit Varma recognised the YouTuber’s logic: “So what if I broke my ankle? Content mila.” {035-J11}

lead.kicker: Ajay Shah, in a cast, on a lifelong love of the hills
lead.head: Broken ankle, unbroken love
body: Amit Varma opened with a truth universally acknowledged: that which we love the most hurts us the most. His fellow cast member, he noted, was in a cast. {035-J01}
Ajay Shah had broken his ankle on a trek in the Sahyadris, his first accident in 45 years of hiking. He asked to save the story for the end, so he could place it within “some bigger principles”.
The hour that followed laid out those principles: why go into the mountains, how to start, how to behave there and when to turn back.
## Built for trees
Shah grew up on the books of Jim Corbett and on accounts of the first ascent of Everest. Mountains and forests, he said, always seemed like “the greatest thing in the world”.
His case for them begins in biology. “As every good biologist will say to you, we are not like monkeys. We are monkeys,” he said. {035-C01}

A life spent among concrete structures, coffee shops and bars, he argued, leaves “a hole in your heart”. Varma put the same thought in a phrase from the poet Dilip Chitre: “man’s estrangement from a man-made world”.
The other reasons came readily: unplugging from email and phones, a beauty no photograph can convey, and the discipline of putting one foot in front of the other for thousands of calories a day.
That is done, Shah said, in a meditative zone where you watch your own breathing, heart and calves. The fitness needed is modest; the real demand is in the mind.
## Love, then the racket

The hosts kept returning to what happens when a pastime becomes a performance. Varma told of pedestrianism, competitive walking, which he said was America’s biggest spectator sport for twenty years before it became a contest to stay awake.
Shah summed it up: “It is the fate of every great idea to start out as a movement and then become a business and then become a racket.”
Varma’s antidote came from the chess grandmaster Tigran Petrosian, who, asked whether he was playing to win or to draw, said he was “playing to play”.

Shah had made the same point earlier about the hardest call in the mountains, when to turn back. Years of training are a sunk cost, and a summit photo for Facebook is no reason to go on. “Life is not lived as a performance to show other people,” he said. {035-C04}
## Never relax
On the trail, he asked for manners: no litter, no Bluetooth speakers, and talk in hushed whispers, so the birds come closer.

Then came the ankle. After a long day’s climb up Tung, Shah relaxed at a chai shop over fresh lime soda, not knowing that 300 metres of descent still lay between him and the lake where they would camp. In failing light, his group followed a pipe downhill, and he fell.
“You can never let your guard down,” he said. “You have to be there with full presence and energy.” {035-C12}
Varma recalled Tom Vanderbilt’s *Traffic*, which found that most accidents happen close to home, when the brain switches off.
Asked how hiking had shaped him, Shah said he could not imagine himself without it. “If I had not been an economist, I would be a biologist.” {035-J18}

second.label: A chess parable
second.head: Neither win nor draw
second.deck: A chess story Amit Varma offers as everybody’s philosophy for life
body: An opponent who badly wanted a draw once leaned forward to test the waters with Tigran Petrosian, the great grandmaster and pioneer of the exchange sacrifice. Was he playing to win? No. To draw? No. Then why was he playing? {035-S05}
“I’m playing to play,” Petrosian said. Amit Varma, who told the story, wanted it adopted as a creed: “I’m hiking to hike. I’m walking to walk. Nothing else kind of matters.”

Ajay Shah said competition had never crept into his own mountain life, and called rock-climbing races “nonsense”. Climbing is meant to be an isolated, ascetic project in which you solve a mountain, he said, like a crossword. {#crossword}

quote.text: This should be everybody’s philosophy for life, that it is not about the win, it is not about the result.

second.caption: playing to play

third.head: Old legs, young laggards
body: Ajay Shah and his friend KP Krishnan once went hiking to Panchachuli, near the India-China border in Uttarakhand. Their companions were a band of teenage boys and girls from Bangalore.

The two older men assumed they would be the weakest link of the chain. Instead they were among the strongest. The teenagers’ lack of fitness, Shah said, was outrageous: their lives were spent sitting on their butts with video games and Netflix.
“It is really a new revelation for me,” he said. “The idea that you can be young and not physically active.” {035-S07}

The story was Shah’s answer to Amit Varma, who had taken an earlier jibe about Netflix personally. “My question for you is on whose butt should I sit,” Varma had asked. “I’ll sit on my butt only, no?” {035-J08}
third.caption: the Bangalore teenagers

p2.title: Why we walk
p2.deck: Ajay Shah’s case for the mountains, from a childhood of Jim Corbett to a cast, as questioned by Amit Varma

sections.label: The first love
sections.head: A boy, a book and a mountain
sections.caption: a lifelong love of the hills
body: Ajay Shah has been going into the mountains since he was 13, and never stopped. Many people, he said, give up in their teens and twenties. “I just kept going.” {035-S01}
Reading planted the seed. Move *For Whom the Bell Tolls*, one of the great books of the world, to a purely urban setting, Shah said, and “the oomph is lost”. {035-R06}

At IIT Bombay in the early 1980s he found a community ready-made. A physics professor, Professor Mahajan, had led the building of a mountaineering culture there. Gear was scarce, so it was pooled, and know-how was handed down. Today, Shah said, the internet, GPS and cheap gear do that job.
## The hole in the heart
Amit Varma asked whether embracing nature makes you a different person, borrowing Dilip Chitre’s phrase “man’s estrangement from a man-made world”. {035-R09}
Shah said yes. Modern thinking, he said, has stretched Karl Marx’s idea of alienation beyond the assembly-line worker: we are monkeys, meant to live among trees. {035-C01}

When Varma, looking at each camera in turn, warned that the hosts were not fans of Marx, Shah disagreed slightly. Marx, he said, was first to see how the market economy is a “wild west wind” that tears down feudalism. {035-C02}
~ He was wrong, Shah added, on essentially every remedy. Varma replied that getting the description right and the prescription wrong is practically part of leftism.

quote.text: I’ve been going out into the mountains from age 13 and I’ve just consistently gone back.

sections.label: The why
sections.head: Hiking to hike
sections.caption: why anyone climbs
body: Amit Varma had long been fascinated by the bodies preserved on Everest, among them the one in the famous Green Boots photograph. Why, he asked, do people climb at all? {#greenboots}

Ajay Shah said he could give lots of ex post reasoning, and “maybe it is all contrived”. As a child he simply had to go out into forests and mountains. Being away from email and phones, he said, calms the mind and makes you think.
There is beauty: the sunrise at Panchachuli, the pawprints of snow leopards. A keen photographer, he said nothing can reproduce the 3D sensation of being there. {#photo}
## The mind you carry
There is also the physical discipline of walking for hours in a meditative zone. His friend KP Krishnan recites thousands of Sanskrit shlokas as he goes.
Perhaps, Shah said, *Zen and the Art of Motorcycle Maintenance* has it right: the Zen you find in the mountain is the Zen that you take up there. {035-R10}
~ What spoils it is performance. Competition had never crept into his own life with the forests and mountains, Shah said; for him it has been “a zone of purity”.

quote.text: The Zen you find in the mountain is the Zen that you take up there.
quote.who: Robert M. Pirsig, as quoted by Ajay Shah

sections.label: The how
sections.head: First a day, then forever
sections.caption: the first day hike
body: “We said to gentle reader, get off your butt and read some books,” Ajay Shah said. “Today we’re saying, gentle reader, get off your butt and go take a hike.” {035-J05}
Everyone should start with a day hike, he said: a small backpack, two litres of water, five apples and a route, ideally with people who know it. {#dayhike}

If you reach a summit wishing you did not have to go back the same day, something is turning inside your heart. Pitch a tent. Then two nights, seven, ten. In modern India, he said, tents beat the caves and temples where hikers once slept.
On a north-south route in Maharashtra, he and Ayush Patnaik have looked at each other around day seven and realised they could keep going till Kanyakumari. {035-C08}
## Not a high ask

The fitness needed is modest. A day may burn two, three or four thousand calories, but in stints of up to an hour on gentle slopes, with breaks. If you can row or run for 10 to 20 minutes, you are ready. The demand, Shah said, is in the mind. {035-C06}
~ Loads are another matter. In the Himalayas, porters, mules or the zo, a yak-cow cross, carry them. In Maharashtra you carry your own, between 5 and 15 per cent of body weight. {#load}

quote.text: The demand is in the mind, meaning it’s about the mind being able to handle the body.

sections.label: Dos and don’ts
sections.head: Whisper, and the birds come
sections.caption: manners in the mountains
body: Ajay Shah’s first rule was to come prepared. On easy routes like Triund behind Dharamshala, and on pilgrimages to Gangotri, he has seen people in party clothes in abject misery, inspired by miraculous things seen on YouTube.

Their grandparents were agricultural workers, with the strength that comes from that. “But in today’s world, if you’re sitting on your butt watching Netflix and eating processed food, you’re not ready,” he said. {035-C07}

Then he pleaded. Do not litter: there is nobody to clean up. Do not play music, which carries for hundreds of metres in the silence. Speak in whispers, and the birds and wildlife will come to you. {035-C09}
Wet wipes should be all cotton, he added. Nylon and polyester are plastics, and would pollute the mountains for a thousand years.
## Teammates
The crew carries your load and cooks and washes up at altitude. Treat them as teammates, Shah said, and take no for an answer with a smile, even when the creamer runs out. {035-C10}
Amit Varma observed that the advice is needed only because “we are disgusting in our everyday lives”.
~ When things go wrong, Shah stays calm. Once, atop Harishchandragad, Arul Menezes began howling with kidney stones. “Have you asked Arul before sharing this anecdote?” Varma asked. {035-J10}

quote.text: Treat them like teammates, don’t treat them like your employees.

sections.label: The recco
sections.head: Kit and caboodle
sections.caption: kit, books and water filters
body: Ajay Shah’s books were three by Jim Corbett and two by Jon Krakauer, *Into Thin Air* and *Into the Wild*. Then came the kit.
After a lifetime of hunting for the right equipment, he called the arrival of Decathlon a breakthrough: good gear, readily available and affordable. {#decathlon}
A day hike needs only the backpack lying around your house. For big trips he advises 75 litres, enough for a sleeping bag and clothes; people often buy too small or too big. {#pack}
He strongly encouraged women to hike, for the freedom it brings and the ability to deal with adversity, noting only that women’s backpacks are cut differently.

For water, he loves the LifeStraw bottle: fill it with bad water, suck, and what comes out is cleaner than any tap water in India. {#lifestraw} For planning, he starts with the Indiahikes website and moves to the desktop version of Google Earth.
## The technology of walking
Amit Varma brought an essay by Adam Gopnik, who writes that our backs and arches, “like querulous cabinet ministers, at first complain and then resign”. {#gopnik}
~ Walking for pleasure, Gopnik argues, has depended on technology: gaslight in London, the rule of law, and from the 1980s the Walkman and cushioned sneakers. {035-C14}

quote.text: It is something that is far easier for us to do in modern times

side.boxText: Ajay Shah grew up on Jim Corbett’s books and on accounts of the first ascent of Everest. He recommends three Corbett books in sequence: *Man-eaters of Kumaon*, *The Man-eating Leopard of Rudraprayag* and *Jungle Lore*. “Everybody will enjoy them,” he says. {035-R01}

contQuote.text: So once you get going, it’s really unstoppable and you don’t feel like stopping. You don’t feel like coming back. You can just keep on going forever.

p3.title: Tales from the trail
p3.deck: A fall, a freezing night, a porter’s ferries and a lost bet on Lincoln

stories.start: In the Sayadris, there is a beautiful mountain top that is called Tung
stories.end: the tent is actually up. Never relax until the tent is up
stories.caption: the fall below Tung
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on Tung, a pipe and a broken ankle
stories.head: A lime soda before the fall
body: In the Sahyadris there is a mountain top called Tung. Look north from it, Ajay Shah said, and there is a lake. That lakeside was where his group meant to pitch their tents.

Tung was their second up-and-down climb of the day. From the top they could see the campsite. Shah began to relax: they had done about a thousand metres up and five hundred down, and now, he thought, it got easier. {#thousandup}
Back at the base there was a chai shop. They dawdled over fresh lime soda while the sun went down, thinking only a kilometre or two of flat walking remained.

They were wrong. Had he looked up the elevations of the summit, the base and the lake on Google Earth, Shah said, he would have known there were still 300 metres of descent to go. {#descent} From the top of Tung, which he put at about 1,100 metres, the view had flattened the terrain. {#tung}

They set off late in failing light and got a little lost. A pipe led down to the lake, so they followed it. That was an elementary error, Shah said: people build pipes along the shortest line, which is also the steepest.
Then came the dumb luck. He fell, and broke his ankle: his first accident in 45 years of hiking.

~ The fall itself was luck, he said, but laziness about homework and a lowered guard had made the conditions for it. His notes to self: “Do a little more homework.” And: “Never relax until the tent is up.” {035-S06}
stories.why: Danger peaks when the job feels done. From above, Amit Varma said, the last stretch of a book or an article always seems flat. And Tom Vanderbilt’s *Traffic* found that most accidents happen close to home. {035-R12}
stories.postscript: Of the cast itself, Shah had no good word: “The cast has no redeeming features.” {#cast}

stories.start: The last place where you pitch tent is called Lamune
stories.end: but I made the call that I can't handle this, I'm going back
stories.caption: the cold night at Lamuney
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah at Goechala, and the call to turn back
stories.head: Cold fingers, warm regrets
body: On the Goechala trek, the Sikkim-side approach to Kanchenjunga, Ajay Shah spent the night at the last campsite, Lamuney, perhaps 4,500 or 4,800 metres up. {#lamuney} The wind came up. In merino, fleece and a jacket, inside a sleeping bag, he could not sleep for the cold.
At 4 a.m. they set off in ghostly moonlight, two or three breaths to every step. They reached Goechala 1, with Kanchenjunga before them.
His guide said he could make Goechala 2. Shah said no: his gloves were bad, his fingertips hurt, and it was perhaps minus 10, or minus 20. {#minus}
~ He still wishes he had gone on. “All I know is that at that moment I desperately wanted to go,” he said, “but I made the call that I can’t handle this, I’m going back.” {035-S02}
stories.why: The hardest call in the mountains is when to stop. Every accident on Everest, Shah said, comes down to that judgment, and Jon Krakauer’s *Into Thin Air* shows it on the final summit day. {035-R04}
stories.postscript: Amit Varma, who worries about friends who take risks, was relieved. “You still have your fingers,” he said.

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah’s third year at IIT Bombay, as a porter
stories.head: The coolie who came down first
body: The west face of Harishchandragad, Ajay Shah said, is worse than vertical: Konkan Kada, a cobra-shaped overhang that looks down into the Konkan and almost to the sea.

In his third year at IIT Bombay, the institute made its first successful climb of the face, and Shah was a coolie, carrying food, water and climbing stores. He made two endless ferries up and down with 20 kg tied to his hip. {035-S03}
“I have not done much technical climbing myself,” he said. “I was just a user of other people’s rope systems.”

~ On the last day he was first out. He rappelled about 1,800 feet through sheer overhang, and at each stop the rope’s natural twist spun him through 360 degrees, so he took photographs all around. {#rappel}
stories.why: You need not be the star to be part of something historic. Carrying food, water and climbing stores for someone else’s climb gave Ajay Shah what he called “another memorable life experience”.

stories.caption: Edward Weston’s walk
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on Edward Weston and the six-day walkers
stories.head: Lincoln won, so Weston walked
body: Amit Varma took the story from Matthew Algeo’s *Pedestrianism*. In 1860, Edward Weston bet a friend that if Lincoln won, he would walk from the State House in Boston to the Capitol in Washington in ten days. {#weston}
Lincoln won. Weston walked, arrived late and missed the inauguration, but the whole country followed him. Then he decided walking should be a competitive sport.

For twenty years it was America’s biggest spectator sport. {#twenty} Crowds paid to watch men go round and round six days a week. Weston, in hunting boots and breeches, was its Federer; the Irish working man Dan O’Leary its Nadal; O’Leary’s protégé Frank Hart, “Black Dan”, a third pillar.

~ Early on, fans compared Weston’s long strides with O’Leary’s shorter, lighter steps. Later technique stopped mattering. “It becomes a battle of staying awake,” Varma said. “They are fighting sleep.” {035-S04}
stories.why: Varma said an activity done for love can turn competitive, then a spectacle, then toxic. Ajay Shah’s summary: every great idea starts as a movement, becomes a business, then becomes a racket. {035-C05}
stories.postscript: Varma imagines the old champions, once the sport died, walking alone again and rediscovering why they loved it.

quiz.a: “I’m playing to play”, which Amit Varma offered as everybody’s philosophy for life.
